calibration.easy: A fact the lesson states plainly. Big-O and defined terms (index) allowed. No operation to perform, no 'why'.
calibration.medium: Do or trace exactly one operation.
calibration.hard: Justify a trade-off or reason about an edge case, strictly within the concept's scope.

concepts.name: Arrays
concepts.lesson:
An array stores a list of elements in one continuous block of memory, side by side. Each element has a position number called its **index**, and indexes usually start at 0. Because the memory is continuous, the computer can jump straight to any element from its index, so reading by index is **O(1)** (one step) no matter how big the array is.

The cost shows up when you change the shape. Inserting or deleting in the middle or at the front means every element after that spot has to shift over, which is **O(n)**. A *fixed-size* array has its size set when it's created; a *dynamic* array can grow. A *2D array* like grid[3][4] is just rows of arrays — 3 rows of 4, so 12 elements — and grid[r][c] is still O(1) because the position is computed from the row, column, and row length.

Example: in [10,20,30,40], deleting index 1 leaves [10,30,40] after the shift. Reversing in place (swap element i with the mirror element at the other end) needs no extra memory.

concepts.name: Linked Lists
concepts.lesson:
A linked list is a chain of **nodes**. Each node holds a piece of data and a **pointer** to the next node. The first node is the **head**; the last points to nothing. Unlike an array, the nodes are not side by side in memory — they're linked only by their pointers.

That design flips the cost trade-off. There is no jumping straight to the nth element: to reach it you start at the head and follow pointers one by one, which is **O(n)**. But if you already hold a node, inserting or deleting next to it is **O(1)** — you just rewire a couple of pointers, no shifting. A *singly* linked list points only forward; a *doubly* linked list also points back to the previous node, which makes backward movement and deletion easier but uses a little more memory per node.

Rule of thumb: arrays win when you mostly read by position; linked lists win when you mostly insert/delete at known points and don't need random access.

Example: in A→B→C, to insert X after A you set A's pointer to X and X's pointer to B, giving A→X→B→C.

concepts.name: Stacks
concepts.lesson:
A stack is a collection where you only ever touch one end: the **top**. It follows **LIFO** — Last In, First Out — like a pile of plates where you add and remove from the top. The three operations are **push** (add to the top), **pop** (remove the top), and **peek** (look at the top without removing it). All three are **O(1)**.

A stack can be built on an array or a linked list. The array version is simple and fast but may need resizing if it fills; the linked version grows freely but spends a little extra memory on pointers.

Stacks fit any situation where the most recent thing should be handled first: the **call stack** (the function called last returns first), **undo** in an editor (the last action is undone first), checking **balanced parentheses**, and **expression evaluation**.

Example: push 1, push 2, push 3. The stack top to bottom is 3,2,1. A single pop returns 3.

concepts.name: Queues
concepts.lesson:
A queue is a collection where you add at one end and remove at the other, like a line of people. It follows **FIFO** — First In, First Out. Adding is **enqueue** (at the back); removing is **dequeue** (from the front). Both are **O(1)**.

If you build a queue on a plain array and keep dequeuing from the front, the freed front slots get stranded — they can't be reused without shifting everything. A **circular queue** solves this: when the back reaches the end of the array it wraps around to reuse those freed front slots. A linked-list queue avoids the problem differently by growing freely, at the cost of extra pointer memory.

Queues fit anything served in arrival order: **job scheduling**, print queues, and **breadth-first search (BFS)**, where nodes are explored in the order they were discovered.

Example: enqueue 1, 2, 3. A dequeue returns 1 (the first one in). The front is now 2.

concepts.name: Hash Tables
concepts.lesson:
A hash table stores key-value pairs and finds them fast. It runs the **key** through a **hash function** that produces a **bucket** (a slot number), and the value is stored there. To look something up, it hashes the key again and goes straight to that bucket — so average lookup and insert are **O(1)**.

The catch is **collisions**: two different keys can hash to the same bucket. Two common fixes: **chaining** stores all colliding items in a small list at that bucket; **open addressing** probes for the next free slot. The **load factor** (items ÷ buckets) measures how full the table is. As it rises, collisions rise, and operations slow down. In the worst case — a bad hash function sending most keys to one bucket — lookup degrades to scanning a list, which is **O(n)**, losing the whole advantage.

Example: with hash(key) = key mod 5, the key 12 lands in bucket 2 (12 mod 5 = 2). If another key also gives bucket 2, that's a collision.

concepts.name: Trees
concepts.lesson:
A tree is a branching structure of nodes. The top node is the **root**; a node with no children is a **leaf**. A node's **depth** is its distance from the root, and the tree's **height** is the longest root-to-leaf distance. In a **binary tree**, each node has at most two children.

A **binary search tree (BST)** adds a rule: for every node, smaller values go in its left subtree and larger values in its right. That rule makes searching efficient — at each step you go left or right, so search and insert cost **O(h)**, where h is the height. Three traversal orders matter: **in-order** (left, node, right) visits a BST's values in sorted order; **pre-order** visits the node before its subtrees; **post-order** visits the subtrees first.

The danger: if values are inserted already sorted, the tree grows in one direction — **skewed**, like a linked list — and search becomes O(n). A **balanced** tree keeps height near log n, so search stays O(log n).

Example: insert 5, then 3, then 8. 3 < 5 so it becomes 5's left child; 8 > 5 so it becomes the right child.

concepts.name: Graphs
concepts.lesson:
A graph is a set of **vertices** (nodes) joined by **edges** (connections). Edges can be **directed** (one-way, A→B) or **undirected** (two-way), and **weighted** edges carry a value or cost. A **path** is a sequence of edges from one vertex to another; a **cycle** is a path that returns to where it started; a graph is **connected** if every vertex can be reached from every other.

Two ways to store a graph: an **adjacency matrix** is an n×n grid marking which vertices connect — checking a specific edge is O(1), but it always uses O(n²) space even when there are few edges. An **adjacency list** stores, for each vertex, only the edges it actually has — saving memory for sparse graphs (few edges), though edge checks are slower.

Two ways to explore: **breadth-first search (BFS)** uses a **queue** to fan out level by level, visiting nearest vertices first; **depth-first search (DFS)** uses a **stack** (or recursion) to go as deep as possible before backtracking.

Example: BFS from a start vertex visits all its direct neighbours before going any further out.
